definition: Real and definite enough to be seen, measured, or touched, rather than vague or imagined.
example: After months of rehearsals, the choir finally heard a tangible improvement in its pitch.
nuance: Palpable often describes a mood felt in the air; tangible more often describes results or evidence you can point to or measure.
prompt: A town council reviews its new recycling program after its first full year.
options: The program produced tangible savings, cutting the town's landfill bill by a third.
The program's gains were tangible, though no one could point to a single one.
Councilor Reyes is quite tangible and runs her fingers over every bin she inspects.
A tangible speech about one member's beach vacation drifted far from the subject of recycling.
reasons: A specific, measurable drop in costs is exactly the kind of concrete result the word describes.
If no one can identify any gain, the benefits are imaginary, which is the reverse of tangible.
A person who loves touching things is tactile; tangible describes things that can be touched or measured.
This confuses the word with tangential, which describes remarks that wander off topic.

practice.prompt: A student wants to show her parents that her math tutoring is paying off.
options: Her tutor is very tangible, so he always arrives early and stays late.
Her report card offered tangible proof, since her grade rose from a C to a B.
The improvement was tangible, so her parents had no way to notice or measure it.
Her headphone cord became tangible after a week stuffed in the bottom of her backpack.
reasons: Being punctual or dependable is a matter of reliability, not of being real and measurable.
A higher grade on paper is solid evidence that anyone can see and check.
Something tangible is easy to notice and measure; this sentence flips the meaning.
This mixes the word up with tangled; a knotted cord has nothing to do with being concrete.
